name: Pancragen

lead: Pancragen (Lys-Glu-Asp-Trp) is a four-amino-acid peptide from Khavinson's group in Saint Petersburg, designed to target pancreatic tissue. Bioregulator users take it for metabolic and ageing support, not for a particular look.

The chain runs from pancreas-targeted effects to metabolic support to healthier metabolism. It raised expression of differentiation factors in pancreatic cell cultures, and has been studied in diabetic rats and aged rhesus monkeys. One small study in older people reported lower fasting glucose and insulin resistance index in treated patients. Nearly all work comes from the developing group.

paras: It is used in periodic courses within longevity routines, often alongside other bioregulator peptides.
Human safety data are very limited, and it is not an approved drug in Western countries.

angle.text: Pancragen is a Khavinson tetrapeptide designed to target pancreatic tissue, used in bioregulator circles for metabolic and ageing support. A small human study reported lower fasting glucose; appearance has not been measured.

lead: Pancragen is a synthetic tetrapeptide (Lys-Glu-Asp-Trp, abbreviated KEDW, usually amidated) developed by Vladimir Khavinson and colleagues at the Saint Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology, designed to act on pancreatic tissue [1]. It belongs to the short-peptide bioregulators that the group proposes as tissue-specific regulators of cell function in ageing [1][2].

Peptides of this family are presented by their developers as tissue-specific regulators of ageing, with the broader aim of keeping organs functioning well with age. Pancragen's own published work concerns pancreatic function and glucose metabolism rather than skin, hair or physique, so any link to appearance runs through that general anti-ageing framing.

Research includes cell cultures in which it raised expression of differentiation factors in pancreatic cells [3][3], streptozotocin-diabetic rats [4], aged rhesus monkeys [5][6] and one small study in older people with and without type 2 diabetes, which reported lower fasting glucose and insulin resistance index in treated patients [7]. Nearly all published work comes from the developing group.

paras: Vladimir Khavinson (1946-2024) was a Russian gerontologist who directed the Saint Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology and chaired gerontology and geriatrics at North-Western State Medical University [2]. His laboratory developed short peptides modelled on fragments extracted from animal organs, which it proposed as tissue-specific bioregulators. His Wikipedia biography credits him with six peptide pharmaceuticals and dozens of peptide food supplements, including Thymalin, Epithalamin and Cortexin, first used in Soviet and Russian military medicine, and notes that it carries a promotional-content flag [2].

Pancragen is the pancreas-directed member of this family. Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, describes it as a synthetic analogue of a natural tetrapeptide from bovine pancreas, with studies appearing from the mid-2000s [8].

A 2011 study examined 30 healthy older persons and 33 older patients with type 2 diabetes. Nocturnal melatonin production was about 70 percent lower in patients than in healthy people, and in patients given Pancragen, fasting glucose, glucose tolerance test values, insulin and insulin resistance index fell, while untreated patients showed no such changes [7]. The study was small, and independent replication is not documented.

In cultured pancreatic cells, Pancragen raised expression of differentiation factors for acinar and islet cells, with effects reported in both young and aged cultures; the authors suggested this could underlie anti-diabetic and anti-inflammatory effects [1][3]. Related work found tissue-specific stimulation of CXCL12 and Hoxa3 in pancreatic cell cultures [3]. A 2006 study reported tissue-specific effects of several synthetic peptide bioregulators in organ cultures from young and old rats [9].

In rats with streptozotocin-induced diabetes, oral Pancragen produced a hypoglycaemic effect and intramuscular administration normalised capillary adhesion, without changing capillary permeability [4]. Russian reports described correction of impaired glucose tolerance and effects on endocrine pancreatic function in old rhesus monkeys [5][6].

Khavinson's institute developed a large family of short peptide products, including Epitalon, and his Wikipedia biography credits him with dozens of peptide food supplements alongside the pharmaceuticals approved in Russia and neighbouring countries [2]. Pancragen is not an approved drug in Western countries, and published human data on safety are limited to the small 2011 study [7].

Pancragen is a four-residue peptide of lysine, glutamic acid, aspartic acid and tryptophan [1]. Its developers describe it as one of a series of short peptides that act in a tissue-specific way, a proposal tested mainly in their own cell-culture work [3][3].
